board_events.text: Four self-referential square matrices
Idempotent: $A^{2}=A$ — applying it twice changes nothing, so $A^{n}=A$.
Involutory: $A^{2}=I$ — its own inverse, $A^{-1}=A$ (a mirror flip).
Nilpotent: $A^{k}=O$ for some $k$; the smallest such $k$ is the index.
Idempotent: $I-A$ is also idempotent; the only invertible idempotent is $I$.
Involutory: even powers give $I$, odd powers give $A$.
Nilpotent matrices are never invertible.
Orthogonal: rows (and columns) are mutually perpendicular unit vectors — rotations.

segments.text: <curious>Beyond the core operations, a handful of square matrices have a self-referential personality — square them, or multiply by their own transpose, and something remarkably simple comes back. Four types matter for JEE.

First, idempotent: A squared equals A. Such a matrix is absorbed by repetition — apply it once and applying it again changes nothing, so every power A to the n is just A again. Think of a projection: casting a shadow twice gives the same shadow.
Second, involutory: A squared equals I. The matrix is its own inverse, so A inverse equals A. Applying it twice undoes it — like a mirror flip.
Third, nilpotent: some power A to the k equals the zero matrix. The smallest such k is called the index. A nilpotent matrix eventually annihilates everything.
Fourth, orthogonal: A times A transpose, and A transpose times A, both equal the identity — which means the inverse is simply the transpose, A inverse equals A transpose.
Each carries a consequence. For an idempotent A, the matrix I minus A is also idempotent, and the only invertible idempotent matrix is the identity itself.
For an involutory matrix, powers alternate cleanly: even powers give the identity, odd powers give A.
A nilpotent matrix can never be invertible — a matrix that eventually sends everything to zero has no undo.
And an orthogonal matrix has rows, and columns, that are mutually perpendicular unit vectors; rotations are the classic example, and its inverse is free to write down.

<curious>core operations से आगे, कुछ square matrices का एक self-referential personality होता है — उन्हें square करो, या अपने ही transpose से multiply करो, और कुछ remarkably simple वापस आता है। JEE के लिए चार types matter करते हैं।

पहला, idempotent: A squared equals A। ऐसी matrix repetition से absorb हो जाती है — एक बार apply करो और दोबारा apply करने से कुछ नहीं बदलता, तो हर power A to the n बस फिर से A है। एक projection सोचो: shadow दो बार डालो तो वही shadow मिलता है।
दूसरा, involutory: A squared equals I। matrix अपना ही inverse है, तो A inverse equals A। इसे दो बार apply करना इसे undo कर देता है — एक mirror flip की तरह।
तीसरा, nilpotent: कोई power A to the k, zero matrix के बराबर। सबसे छोटा ऐसा k index कहलाता है। एक nilpotent matrix आख़िरकार सब कुछ annihilate कर देती है।
चौथा, orthogonal: A times A transpose, और A transpose times A, दोनों identity के बराबर — यानी inverse बस transpose है, A inverse equals A transpose।
हर एक एक consequence लाता है। idempotent A के लिए, matrix I minus A भी idempotent है, और एकमात्र invertible idempotent matrix खुद identity है।
involutory matrix के लिए, powers साफ़-साफ़ alternate करती हैं: even powers identity देती हैं, odd powers A देती हैं।
एक nilpotent matrix कभी invertible नहीं हो सकती — जो matrix आख़िरकार सब कुछ zero भेज देती है उसका कोई undo नहीं।
और एक orthogonal matrix की rows, और columns, mutually perpendicular unit vectors होती हैं; rotations classic example हैं, और इसका inverse लिखना free है।

sections.title: The trace of a square matrix

board_events.text: The trace of a square matrix
Surprising: $AB\ne BA$ in general, yet their traces always agree.
So $\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0$ always — a favourite JEE one-liner.
Trace is linear: it distributes over sums and pulls out scalars.

segments.text: One number captures a lot about a square matrix: its trace.
The trace is simply the sum of the diagonal entries — a one one plus a two two, all the way down.
It behaves linearly. The trace of a sum is the sum of the traces.
A scalar pulls straight out — trace of k A is k times trace of A — and transposing changes nothing, since the diagonal is untouched: trace of A transpose equals trace of A.
And the surprising identity: the trace of A B equals the trace of B A.
That one is a genuine shock, because A B and B A are usually different matrices — yet their diagonals always sum to the same number.
A direct consequence the examiners love: the trace of A B minus B A is always zero. It is a favourite one-line trap.
So hold the trace as a linear gadget: it distributes over sums, pulls out scalars, ignores transposes, and cannot tell A B from B A.
एक number एक square matrix के बारे में बहुत कुछ capture करता है: उसका trace।
trace बस diagonal entries का sum है — a one one plus a two two, नीचे तक।
ये linearly behave करता है। sum का trace, traces का sum है।
एक scalar सीधे बाहर निकल आता है — k A का trace, k times trace of A है — और transpose करने से कुछ नहीं बदलता, क्योंकि diagonal अछूता रहता है: A transpose का trace, trace of A के बराबर है।
और वो surprising identity: A B का trace, B A के trace के बराबर है।
ये वाला सच में shock है, क्योंकि A B और B A आम तौर पर अलग matrices हैं — फिर भी उनके diagonals हमेशा एक ही number तक sum होते हैं।
एक सीधा consequence जो examiners को पसंद है: A B minus B A का trace हमेशा zero होता है। ये एक favourite one-line trap है।
तो trace को एक linear gadget की तरह पकड़ो: ये sums पर distribute होता है, scalars बाहर खींचता है, transposes को ignore करता है, और A B को B A से अलग नहीं बता सकता।

sections.title: Evaluating a polynomial at a matrix

board_events.text: Evaluating a polynomial at a matrix
Replace $x$ by $A$ and the constant $c$ by $cI$ — that is $f(A)$.
A square matrix very often satisfies an equation $f(A)=O$ of its own.
That single fact unlocks high powers AND the inverse — cheaply.
For the inverse: rearrange to $A\,(\text{poly})=cI$, then divide by $c$.
For high powers: use the relation to reduce $A^{2}$ (or higher) to lower terms.

segments.text: Here is one of the most powerful ideas in the chapter: you can feed a matrix into a polynomial.
Just replace the variable x by the matrix A, and replace the constant term c by c times the identity. That gives f of A.
For example, if f of x is x squared minus two x minus three, then f of A is A squared minus two A minus three I — the plain three becomes three times the identity.
The remarkable thing is that a square matrix very often satisfies a polynomial equation of its own — some f of A equals the zero matrix.
And that single relation is a master key: it unlocks both high powers of A and the inverse of A, with almost no computation.
For the inverse, rearrange the relation into A times some polynomial equals c times the identity, then divide by that non-zero c — exactly the trick from the last subtopic.
For high powers, use the relation to rewrite A squared, or higher, in terms of lower powers, and cascade downward.
For instance, if A squared equals two A plus three I, then A cubed is A times A squared, which becomes two A squared plus three A — and you keep collapsing, no brute force needed.
यहाँ chapter के सबसे powerful ideas में से एक है: तुम एक matrix को polynomial में feed कर सकते हो।
बस variable x को matrix A से replace करो, और constant term c को c times identity से। इससे f of A मिलता है।
मिसाल के लिए, अगर f of x है x squared minus two x minus three, तो f of A है A squared minus two A minus three I — plain three, three times identity बन जाता है।
remarkable बात ये है कि एक square matrix अक्सर अपनी ही एक polynomial equation satisfy करती है — कोई f of A, zero matrix के बराबर।
और वो एक relation एक master key है: ये A की high powers और A का inverse, दोनों unlock कर देती है, लगभग बिना computation।
inverse के लिए, relation को A times कोई polynomial equals c times identity में rearrange करो, फिर उस non-zero c से divide करो — बिल्कुल पिछले subtopic वाला trick।
high powers के लिए, relation use करके A squared, या उससे ऊपर, को lower powers में rewrite करो, और नीचे की तरफ cascade करो।
मिसाल के लिए, अगर A squared equals two A plus three I, तो A cubed है A times A squared, जो बन जाता है two A squared plus three A — और तुम collapse करते जाते हो, कोई brute force नहीं चाहिए।

sections.title: Special types, trace, and polynomials — the rulebook

board_events.text: Special types, trace, polynomials — the rulebook
Idempotent: $A^{n}=A$. Involutory: even $\to I$, odd $\to A$.

segments.text: The consolidated rulebook for this subtopic — the definitions and identities you actually reach for.
The self-referential types: idempotent means A squared equals A; involutory means A squared equals I, so the matrix is its own inverse.
Nilpotent means some power A to the k is the zero matrix — and such a matrix is never invertible; orthogonal means A times A transpose is the identity, so the inverse is just the transpose.
The trace: the sum of diagonal entries, linear over sums, and it pulls scalars out.
Two more trace facts: it is unchanged by transposing, and the trace of A B equals the trace of B A even when the products differ.
Evaluating a polynomial at a matrix: replace the variable by A, and every constant by that constant times the identity.
And the inverse trick in one line: if f of A is the zero matrix, rearrange to A times a polynomial equals c times I, then A inverse is one over c times that polynomial.
Two power shortcuts to bank: for an idempotent matrix every power is just A; for an involutory matrix, even powers give the identity and odd powers give A.
इस subtopic के लिए consolidated rulebook — वो definitions और identities जो तुम असल में इस्तेमाल करते हो।
self-referential types: idempotent का मतलब A squared equals A; involutory का मतलब A squared equals I, तो matrix अपना ही inverse है।
Nilpotent का मतलब कोई power A to the k, zero matrix है — और ऐसी matrix कभी invertible नहीं; orthogonal का मतलब A times A transpose identity है, तो inverse बस transpose है।
trace: diagonal entries का sum, sums पर linear, और ये scalars बाहर खींचता है।
दो और trace facts: transpose करने से ये unchanged रहता है, और A B का trace, B A के trace के बराबर है, भले ही products अलग हों।
matrix पर polynomial evaluate करना: variable को A से replace करो, और हर constant को उस constant times identity से।
और inverse trick one line में: अगर f of A zero matrix है, A times a polynomial equals c times I में rearrange करो, फिर A inverse है one over c times वो polynomial।
बैंक करने लायक दो power shortcuts: idempotent matrix के लिए हर power बस A है; involutory matrix के लिए, even powers identity देती हैं और odd powers A।

board_events.text: Worked example: verify $f(A)=O$, then invert
Now exploit it: from $A^{2}-2A-3I=O$, isolate a factor of $A$.
One identity gives both the verification AND the inverse — no row reduction.

segments.text: Now we put matrix polynomials to work, on a problem that first verifies an identity and then uses it to invert.
The matrix is A equals one, two, two, one, and we must show A squared minus two A minus three I is the zero matrix, then find A inverse.
Square A first. Multiply it by itself: A squared comes out five, four, four, five.
Write the other pieces: two A is two, four, four, two; and three I is three, zero, zero, three.
Now combine entrywise: five minus two minus three is zero on the diagonal, and four minus four is zero off it — the whole thing is the zero matrix. The identity is verified.
Now exploit that relation to invert. Start from A squared minus two A minus three I equals zero, and isolate a factor of A.

Move the three I across: A squared minus two A equals three I. Factor A on the left: A times the quantity A minus two I equals three I. Divide by three: A times one-third of A minus two I equals the identity.
So A inverse is one-third of A minus two I, which works out to minus one-third, two-thirds, two-thirds, minus one-third.
One identity delivered both the verification and the inverse — not a single row operation needed.
अब हम matrix polynomials को काम पर लगाते हैं, एक ऐसे problem पर जो पहले एक identity verify करता है और फिर उसे invert करने के लिए इस्तेमाल करता है।
matrix है A equals one, two, two, one, और हमें दिखाना है कि A squared minus two A minus three I zero matrix है, फिर A inverse निकालना है।
पहले A square करो। इसे खुद से multiply करो: A squared निकलता है five, four, four, five।
बाकी pieces लिखो: two A है two, four, four, two; और three I है three, zero, zero, three।
अब entrywise combine करो: diagonal पर five minus two minus three, zero है, और off-diagonal पर four minus four, zero — पूरी चीज़ zero matrix है। identity verify हो गई।
अब उस relation को invert करने के लिए exploit करो। A squared minus two A minus three I equals zero से शुरू करो, और A का एक factor isolate करो।

three I को across ले जाओ: A squared minus two A equals three I। left पर A factor करो: A times the quantity A minus two I equals three I। three से divide करो: A times one-third of A minus two I equals identity।
तो A inverse है one-third of A minus two I, जो निकलता है minus one-third, two-thirds, two-thirds, minus one-third।
एक identity ने verification और inverse, दोनों दे दिए — एक भी row operation की ज़रूरत नहीं।

board_events.text: Worked example: simplify using $A^{2}=A$
Idempotence collapses every power of $A$ back to $A$; $I$ commutes with all.
The $-7A$ term is engineered to cancel the collapse exactly.
Answer: $I$. No entries, no order given — pure structure.

segments.text: This one shows how a defining property turns a scary expansion into a one-liner. A is idempotent, and we simplify the cube of I plus A, minus seven A.
The setup: A squared equals A. That is the only fact we use.
The key: idempotence collapses every power of A back to A, and the identity commutes with everything, so the binomial expansion behaves exactly like ordinary algebra here.
Expand the cube of I plus A: it is I plus three A plus three A squared plus A cubed.
Now collapse the powers. A squared is A, and A cubed is also A, so three A squared plus A cubed becomes three A plus A, four A in total — the whole cube is I plus seven A.
Subtract the seven A: I plus seven A minus seven A leaves exactly the identity.
Notice the problem was engineered — the minus seven A term is precisely what cancels the collapsed expansion.
The answer is simply I, reached with no entries and no order given at all — pure structure.
ये दिखाता है कि एक defining property कैसे एक डरावने expansion को one-liner बना देती है। A idempotent है, और हम I plus A के cube, minus seven A को simplify करते हैं।
setup: A squared equals A। बस यही एक fact हम use करते हैं।
key: idempotence, A की हर power को वापस A में collapse कर देती है, और identity हर चीज़ से commute करती है, तो यहाँ binomial expansion बिल्कुल ordinary algebra की तरह behave करता है।
I plus A के cube को expand करो: ये है I plus three A plus three A squared plus A cubed।
अब powers collapse करो। A squared, A है, और A cubed भी A है, तो three A squared plus A cubed बन जाता है three A plus A, कुल four A — पूरा cube है I plus seven A।
seven A subtract करो: I plus seven A minus seven A से exactly identity बचता है।
गौर करो problem engineered था — minus seven A term ठीक वही है जो collapsed expansion को cancel करता है।
answer बस I है, बिना किसी entry और बिना कोई order दिए पहुँचा — pure structure।

board_events.text: Worked example: a real sales model
(i) Total units per product = add the two month-rows.
So 75 pens, 55 notebooks, 50 erasers.
(ii) Revenue per month = $Mp$ (units times prices).
Addition gives 'totals'; multiplication gives 'units $\times$ price' — the operations are the model.

segments.text: To close the subtopic, a genuinely applied problem — the kind CBSE asks for four to six marks — showing that the operations are not decorative, they are the model.

A stationery seller records two months of unit sales of three products — pens, notebooks, erasers — as a matrix M, with months as rows and products as columns. The selling prices form a column vector p: fifty, twenty, ten rupees.
Part one asks for the total units sold of each product. Since the two rows are the two months, you just add them.
Add row one and row two entrywise: forty plus thirty-five, twenty-five plus thirty, thirty plus twenty — seventy-five, fifty-five, fifty.
So across both months: seventy-five pens, fifty-five notebooks, fifty erasers.
Part two asks for each month's revenue — that is units times prices, which is the matrix product M times p.
Multiply: month one is forty times fifty, plus twenty-five times twenty, plus thirty times ten — two thousand eight hundred. Month two works out to two thousand five hundred fifty.
So month one earns two thousand eight hundred rupees, month two two thousand five hundred fifty, for a grand total of five thousand three hundred fifty.
Notice the division of labour: addition handled the totals, and multiplication handled units times price. The matrix operations are literally the business model.
subtopic close करने के लिए, एक सचमुच applied problem — जैसा CBSE चार से छह marks के लिए पूछता है — दिखाता है कि operations decorative नहीं, वो model हैं।

एक stationery seller तीन products — pens, notebooks, erasers — की दो महीनों की unit sales एक matrix M के रूप में record करता है, months rows में और products columns में। selling prices एक column vector p बनाते हैं: fifty, twenty, ten रुपये।
Part one हर product की कुल बेची गई units पूछता है। चूँकि दोनों rows दो महीने हैं, तुम बस उन्हें add कर देते हो।
row one और row two को entrywise add करो: forty plus thirty-five, twenty-five plus thirty, thirty plus twenty — seventy-five, fifty-five, fifty।
तो दोनों महीनों में: seventy-five pens, fifty-five notebooks, fifty erasers।
Part two हर महीने का revenue पूछता है — यानी units times prices, जो matrix product M times p है।
multiply करो: month one है forty times fifty, plus twenty-five times twenty, plus thirty times ten — two thousand eight hundred। month two निकलता है two thousand five hundred fifty।
तो month one two thousand eight hundred रुपये कमाता है, month two two thousand five hundred fifty, grand total five thousand three hundred fifty।
division of labour देखो: addition ने totals संभाले, और multiplication ने units times price। matrix operations literally business model हैं।

board_events.text: Pro-tips for special matrices
Trace trap: $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$ even though $AB\ne BA$.
Idempotent collapse: every power is $A$, so $A^{n}=A$ — never expand.
Involutory: even powers $\to I$, odd $\to A$; this crushes long power sums.
Nilpotent is always singular; orthogonal gives $A^{-1}=A^{T}$ for free.
Matrix-polynomial: from $f(A)=O$ with non-zero constant, factor out $A$ for $A^{-1}$.
Application problems: addition = totals/combine; multiplication = units $\times$ rate.
Read the property first — it usually replaces all the arithmetic.

segments.text: A cluster of pro-tips that turn these special matrices into fast marks.
The trace trap: remember that the trace of A B equals the trace of B A, even though A B and B A are usually different matrices. Examiners set this precisely to catch the unwary.
Idempotent collapse: if A squared equals A, then every power of A is just A. Never expand — collapse.
Involutory shortcut: even powers give the identity, odd powers give A. This crushes a long sum of powers into a simple head count of odds and evens.
Two more: a nilpotent matrix is always singular, so it has no inverse; and an orthogonal matrix hands you its inverse for free, since A inverse equals A transpose.
The matrix-polynomial move once more: whenever f of A is the zero matrix and the constant term is non-zero, factor out A and read off the inverse directly.
In application problems, map the operation to the meaning: addition combines or totals, and multiplication pairs units with a rate or price.
<whisper>The meta-tip across all of these: read the defining property first. Nine times out of ten it replaces the arithmetic entirely.
pro-tips का एक cluster जो इन special matrices को fast marks में बदल देता है।
trace trap: याद रखो कि A B का trace, B A के trace के बराबर है, भले ही A B और B A आम तौर पर अलग matrices हों। examiners इसे ठीक इसीलिए सेट करते हैं ताकि लापरवाह पकड़े जाएँ।
idempotent collapse: अगर A squared equals A, तो A की हर power बस A है। कभी expand मत करो — collapse करो।
involutory shortcut: even powers identity देती हैं, odd powers A। ये powers के एक लंबे sum को odds और evens की simple head count में कुचल देता है।
दो और: एक nilpotent matrix हमेशा singular है, तो उसका कोई inverse नहीं; और एक orthogonal matrix अपना inverse free में दे देती है, क्योंकि A inverse equals A transpose।
matrix-polynomial move एक बार फिर: जब भी f of A zero matrix हो और constant term non-zero हो, A factor out करके inverse सीधे पढ़ लो।
application problems में, operation को meaning से map करो: addition combine या total करता है, और multiplication units को एक rate या price से pair करता है।
<whisper>इन सबके ऊपर meta-tip: पहले defining property पढ़ो। दस में से नौ बार वो arithmetic को पूरी तरह replace कर देती है।

board_events.text: Your complete Matrices toolkit
$AB\ne BA$; $\ IA=AI=A$; $\ AB=O$ need not give $A=O$ or $B=O$.
Deferred to Ch. 4: the test $|A|\ne0$ and $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{|A|}\,\mathrm{adj}\,A$.

segments.text: <whisper>Here is your complete Matrices toolkit — one board that consolidates the whole chapter. Nothing new; just everything in one place for the final revision.
Representation: build entries from the rule a i j equals f of i j; the number of possible orders is the divisor count of N; and the number of matrices over a k-set is k to the m n.
The three operations: addition and scalar multiplication are entrywise; multiplication is the row-times-column sum over the shared index.
The cautions that ride with multiplication: it is not commutative, the identity leaves a matrix unchanged, and a zero product does not force a zero factor.
The transpose laws: transpose of a transpose is A, it distributes over sums, scalars ride through, and — the crucial one — a product's transpose reverses the order.
Symmetric means A transpose equals A, skew means A transpose equals minus A, and every square matrix is the unique sum of half A plus A transpose and half A minus A transpose.
The entry counts: n times n plus one over two for symmetric, and n times n minus one over two for skew.
The special types — idempotent, involutory, nilpotent, orthogonal — and the trace identity that the trace of A B equals the trace of B A.
The inverse: defined by A times A inverse equals I, the product rule reverses the order, transpose and inverse commute, and the row-reduction method takes A beside I to I beside A inverse.
And one deliberate pointer forward: the determinant test for invertibility and the adjoint formula arrive in the next chapter, Determinants.
<whisper>यहाँ तुम्हारा complete Matrices toolkit है — एक board जो पूरे chapter को consolidate करता है। कुछ नया नहीं; बस final revision के लिए सब कुछ एक जगह।
Representation: entries को rule a i j equals f of i j से बनाओ; possible orders की संख्या N का divisor count है; और k-set के ऊपर matrices की संख्या k to the m n है।
तीनों operations: addition और scalar multiplication entrywise हैं; multiplication shared index के ऊपर row-times-column sum है।
multiplication के साथ चलने वाली cautions: ये commutative नहीं है, identity matrix को unchanged छोड़ती है, और zero product किसी factor को zero नहीं बनाता।
transpose laws: transpose का transpose A है, ये sums पर distribute होता है, scalars साथ चलते हैं, और — crucial वाली — product का transpose order reverse करता है।
Symmetric का मतलब A transpose equals A, skew का मतलब A transpose equals minus A, और हर square matrix, half A plus A transpose और half A minus A transpose का unique sum है।
entry counts: symmetric के लिए n times n plus one over two, और skew के लिए n times n minus one over two।
special types — idempotent, involutory, nilpotent, orthogonal — और वो trace identity कि A B का trace, B A के trace के बराबर है।
inverse: A times A inverse equals I से define, product rule order reverse करता है, transpose और inverse commute करते हैं, और row-reduction method A को I के बगल से I को A inverse के बगल तक ले जाता है।
और एक जानबूझकर pointer आगे के लिए: invertibility के लिए determinant test और adjoint formula अगले chapter, Determinants, में आते हैं।

board_events.text: Rapid-recall cheat sheet
Construct: row $i$ then column $j$; orders = divisors of $N$; matrices = $k^{mn}$.
Multiply: 'inner match, outer survive'; $AB\ne BA$; never cancel a matrix.
'Transpose a product, turn it around': $(AB)^{T}=B^{T}A^{T}$.
'Symmetric adds, skew subtracts' (both over 2); skew's diagonal is asleep.
Special: idempotent $A^{2}=A$, involutory $A^{2}=I$, nilpotent $A^{k}=O$, orthogonal $A^{-1}=A^{T}$.
Inverse: $[A\mid I]\to[I\mid A^{-1}]$; 'zero row, no go'; $(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}$.
Matrix-polynomial: from $A\,(\text{poly})=cI$, divide by $c$ for $A^{-1}$.
Anchors: 'row before column'; 'inner match, outer survive'; 'zero row, no inverse'.
Coming in Ch. 4: the $|A|\ne0$ test and the adjoint inverse.

segments.text: Finally, the rapid-recall card — the one-glance summary to run through the night before the exam.
Representation in a breath: build each entry with the rule, count possible orders as the divisors of N, and count matrices as k to the m n.
Multiplication: inner match, outer survive; A B is not B A; and you can never cancel a matrix out of an equation.
Transpose a product and turn it around — A B transpose is B transpose A transpose.
Symmetric adds, skew subtracts, both over two; and a skew matrix's diagonal is always asleep, all zeros.
The special types at a glance: idempotent A squared equals A, involutory A squared equals I, nilpotent A to the k equals O, orthogonal A inverse equals A transpose.
Inverses by row operations: reduce A beside I to I beside A inverse; zero row, no go; and the product inverse reverses to B inverse A inverse.
The matrix-polynomial shortcut: from A times a polynomial equals c times I, divide by c to get A inverse.
Three anchors to carry into the hall: row before column; inner match, outer survive; and zero row, no inverse.
And a heads-up: the determinant test for invertibility and the adjoint inverse are the very next chapter.
आख़िर में, rapid-recall card — one-glance summary जो exam से एक रात पहले दौड़ा लो।
Representation एक साँस में: हर entry rule से बनाओ, possible orders को N के divisors गिनो, और matrices को k to the m n।
Multiplication: inner match, outer survive; A B, B A नहीं है; और तुम कभी किसी matrix को equation से cancel नहीं कर सकते।
product को transpose करो और उसे turn around करो — A B transpose है B transpose A transpose।
Symmetric adds, skew subtracts, दोनों over two; और skew matrix का diagonal हमेशा सोया रहता है, सब zeros।
special types एक नज़र में: idempotent A squared equals A, involutory A squared equals I, nilpotent A to the k equals O, orthogonal A inverse equals A transpose।
row operations से inverses: A को I के बगल से I को A inverse के बगल तक reduce करो; zero row, no go; और product inverse reverse होकर B inverse A inverse।
matrix-polynomial shortcut: A times a polynomial equals c times I से, c से divide करके A inverse पाओ।
hall में ले जाने के लिए तीन anchors: row before column; inner match, outer survive; और zero row, no inverse।
और एक heads-up: invertibility के लिए determinant test और adjoint inverse बिल्कुल अगला chapter है।
